 7m ago 13.20 EST Which senior Congress members lost reelection?
 An anonymous reader in Seattle asked in a reader callout: Who are the top five most senior representatives who lost reelection?
 double quotation mark Shrai Popat , political reporter and live blogger : One of the biggest lawmakers to lose re-election this cycle was Senator Susan Collins of Maine . She is the five-term Republican incumbent who lost to the progressive Democrat Troy Jackson. It was a stunning end to Collins’ career — she’s spent nearly 30 years in the Senate and really touted her seniority and independence on the trail. Throughout Trump’s time in office, she’s been happy to break with the president and has painted her self as a moderate. She’s also directed millions of dollars back to Maine in her position as appropriations committee chair. In all my conversations with voters, strategists and elected officials in Maine over the last year everyone was genuinely unsure whether Jackson would be able to beat Collins, given how comfortably she’s defied political gravity in the past. She was also the only Republican running for election in a state that Trump lost in 2024, which is further proof that even self-styled independents weren’t immune from the anti-Trump animus that blew Republicans out of the water this cycle.
 View image in fullscreen A sign supporting US Senator Susan Collins (R-ME) for re-election lays fallen on the ground the day after democratic challenger Troy Jackson won the election, in Bangor, Maine, US November 4, 2026. Photograph: Taylor Coester/Reuters 
 double quotation mark Shrai continues: Other big names who lost reelection were Roger Marshall — the incumbent Republican senator from Kansas — who lost to Democrat Adam Hamilton, the pastor of a mega-church, who pulled off an astonishing upset and is now the first Democrat to win a Senate seat in that state in almost a century. Then we have Governor Greg Abbott in Texas, who was vying for a fourth term, but lost to Democratic state rep. Gina Hinojosa — poised to be the first Latina governor of the state. Another big re-election loss happened in Nevada, where Republican governor Joe Lombardo lost to Democrat Aaron Ford, the state’s attorney general. And then there are dozens of House Republicans who lost their re-election races (some of these are reps who managed to win in states that Kamala Harris carried in 2024). Some of the the most striking ones are Tom Kean Jr in New Jersey, Mike Lawler in New York and David Valadao in California.
 What the downfall of near three-decade senator Susan Collins says about Republican unpopularity Read more Share 14m ago 13.12 EST How do the midterms impact the future of the electoral college?
 Bgdxc1 asks in the comments : How will this election impact the implementation of NPVIC? How plausible is it that the bills would impact 2028?
 double quotation mark Sam Levine , voting rights reporter: The mid-term results give the The National Popular Vote Interstate Compact (NPVIC) a serious chance of going into effect. For anyone unfamiliar, the (NPVIC) is an agreement among states in which they agree to award their electoral college votes to the winner of the national popular vote. It would only go into effect if states with at least 270 electoral college votes - enough to win the presidency) agree. Currently, states with 222 electoral votes have agreed to the pact. Democrats won trifectas on Tuesday in states that have 61 electoral votes. Enough states would have to agree to the compact by July 20, 2028 in order for it to go into effect for the next presidential election. Even though Democrats now have enough legislatures to enact the pact, it doesn’t mean it will necessarily go into effect. For one, the states where Democrats have new majorities are the presidential battlegrounds Arizona, Wisconsin, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Michigan. Those states may not be interested in giving up the attention and focus they get in presidential election years and the federal resources that come with it. There are likely to be a slew of legal challenges to the agreement should enough states join and I would expect the US supreme court to have final say on whether such an agreement is constitutional.
 Not just Congress: Democrats’ blue wave washes over state legislatures across US Read more View image in fullscreen Jake Krupa colors in an electoral map as states projected for Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump or Democratic Presidential candidate Hillary Clinton at an election watching party in Coconut Grove, Florida, on November 8, 2016. Photograph: Rhona Wise/AFP/Getty Images Share Updated at  13.13 EST 25m ago 13.02 EST How important was youth turnout?
 Stephen Zunes from Santa Cruz, California asked in a reader callout: How important a factor was youth turnout?
 double quotation mark Lex McMenamin , movement building reporter: For context, I’ve been closely covering the youth vote since 2018, and it was my main beat up until this January. I’ve been back on it this week, and what an exciting one to return! I feel safe saying it as of right now: Based on exit polling, young people were absolutely a decisive voting bloc this cycle — as they have been in the last two midterm cycles. According to Tufts University’s Center for Information & Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE), which monitors youth civic engagement, 2026 youth turnout was the second-highest midterms turnout in 30 years, second only to the 2018 midterms that brought us the Squad during Trump’s first term. Every youth population that went for Trump in 2024, including both Latino and white men, flipped Democratic by several points. They voted blue on average by +30 in battleground states like Florida and Michigan. These numbers may shift slightly by the spring, when CIRCLE will release full voter data — which, as my colleague Will Craft notes below, are not yet available — but are nonetheless historically notable. Young people are a part of a backlash we’re seeing across generations against Republicans, but it’s absolutely about the issues, too: It was over the economy, U.S. war-making, and civil rights. They also won a number of seats in state legislatures, continuing to build a presence in government. I’ll dig into the details, and talk to some of those youth voters, in a story coming this weekend.
 View image in fullscreen Students queue to vote at the University of Texas during the US midterm elections on Election Day, in Austin, Texas, US, November 3, 2026. Photograph: Mike Segar/Reuters 
 double quotation mark Will Craft , data editor: Before I dig into my answer, I want to flag that all the numbers on turnout and vote shifts are estimates right now. Unfortunately we aren’t going to know exactly how different groups voted with a high degree of specificity for a few weeks or months, because as votes are counted and all the election data nerd’s models shift to get more precise. So bear in mind that we don’t know exactly how different groups voted, but we have a decently idea on how they voted. Some places like certain New York city based large news organizations have extremely detailed statistical models telling them how people in different demographics voted, but here at the Guardian we used census data to group counties together based on how many young people there are in the county. Now, not all the young people voted in those counties, but its a decent proxy. What I found was that counties where more than a quarter of the population is under the age of 30, there was a 16 point swing to the Dems.
 But this wasn’t your question! You asked how important the youth turnout was. Here’s my honest answer. There isn’t a single demographic that did not shift to the Dems, and every single one of those demographics shifting is important. The election wasn’t a blue tsunami (bluenami?) because the youth voted Democrat. Or because Hispanic voters went for the Democrats. Or because black voters swung even further to the Democrats. The important factor in this election is that there was a societal wide, top to bottom swing away from the GOP at all levels of government.
 Where Trump and Republicans lost the midterms – a visual analysis of the key states Read more Share Updated at  13.27 EST 35m ago 12.52 EST What changes can actually be implemented regarding ICE, gerrymandering and wars?
 Joyce San Pedro in New York asked in a reader callout: What changes can actually be implemented? Can we undo the Republican gerrymandering? Defund certain wars? Abolish ICE? Impeach Hegseth and Kennedy?
 double quotation mark José Olivares , immigration reporter: The road to Abolish ICE would be a long and difficult one for Democrats.
 It is also not clear whether the push to abolish the agency is a position that all Democrats are united on. For example, Illinois representative Delia Ramirez — one of the most vocal anti-ICE progressive Democrats — has introduced the “Reimagining Safety Act,” which would dismantle the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and abolish ICE. In its place, Ramirez proposes creating the “Department of Community Safety.”
 View image in fullscreen Anti-ICE demonstrators blockade the roadway on the Brooklyn Bridge holding signs that read ‘ABOLISH ICE’ protesting the continued detainment of O. Belgal, who was shot by federal agents in the Bronx with his 5-yr-old son in the car. Photo: Gina M Randazzo/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Photograph: Gina M Randazzo/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock 
 double quotation mark José continues: On the other hand, the more mainstream Democrats and leadership of the party have not explicitly called for abolishing the agency and instead have called for reforms. On Thursday, after the midterms, the House Judiciary Democrats posted on X — to much criticism — that it’s “time for ICE to take the masks off, turn the body cameras on, and start answering to the American people.” Essentially: ICE operations can continue, just without masks and with body cameras.
 If Democrats were united in abolishing ICE, they could galvanize around Ramirez’s legislation. Even then, it would be a big task. DHS, despite it being a young department, carries out a tremendous amount of work and is significantly entrenched in border issues, disaster response, and an increasing role in the federal criminal justice system. Republicans and DHS supporters would put up a ferocious fight to preserve it, and likely accuse Democrats of being “weak on crime” and desiring “open borders.” Would mainstream Democrats and party leadership be able to push through those political accusations to eventually abolish ICE? It’s unknown, but unlikely.
 ‘Abolish ICE’: Mamdani, AOC and other Democrats urge action after New York shooting Read more Share 47m ago 12.40 EST What are the impacts of Democrats flipping state legislatures?
 Jim Garrett in Massachusetts asked in a reader callout: Where have Democrats flipped state legislatures, and what could be the impact of that? Also, what consequential ballot measures have passed?
 double quotation mark Lex McMenamin , movement building reporter : This week in New Hampshire — an important presidential primary battleground state, regardless of its small size — saw a seismic Democratic conquering in both its federal and its state races. More surprising than its congressional outcome for Chris Pappas , whose race was leaning his way before Tuesday, or the Dems winning both US house seats, state Dems flipped the whole state legislature, some 420 seats. New Hampshire’s unique five person statewide executive council, which makes budget and spending decisions, is going from 4-1 conservative control to, for the first time ever, Democrats in all five seats. State Dems were hoping to maybe win the State House; this outcome is one they were totally unprepared for, and will change the state’s agenda over the next two years, laying the groundwork to potentially reverse some anti-LBGTQ laws passed in the last few years of a Republican majority; and finally legalize marijuana, a bipartisan goal.
 View image in fullscreen Chris Pappas meets supporters as he arrives to vote in the US midterm elections in New Hampshire, hours before he was elected to US Senate. Photograph: Kylie Cooper/Reuters Democrat Chris Pappas wins New Hampshire Senate race to become first out gay senator Read more Share 1h ago 12.30 EST Who is likely to run for president in 2028?
 Steven Williams from Kentucky asked in a reader callout: Who do you see as front runners, from both parties, for 2028?
 double quotation mark Lauren Gambino , senior political correspondent: Any Democrat with ambitions of running for president in 2028 could make a case based on the results of 2028. Progressives won, populists won, moderates won, conservative Democrats won - all across the country.
 The names still being discussed are Jon Ossoff, who easily won re-election on Tuesday to his Georgia Senate seat, AOC , who campaigned for many progressives, as well as more moderate figures like NY governor Kathy Hochul . There is already an effort to draft congressman Ro Khanna into the race (though I don’t think that will be very hard!) Kamala Harris campaigned in swing states around the country – and Mississippi, which looks like an incredible move given the nail-biting Senate race there. Gavin Newsom , of course whose bet to redistrict his state is paying off.
 Xavier Becerra wins California race for governor with vows to resist Trump’s agenda Read more 
 double quotation mark On the Republican side, all this maneuvering away from Trump and speaking out about the war can be read as potential 2028 hopefuls thinking about a potential candidacy. JD Vance will likely be considered a contender, but I think Tuesday’s results shattered his frontrunner status a bit. As Kamala Harris knows, its very hard to put distance between an unpopular president having served as their vice president. Ron DeSantis will likely run, Marco Rubio , possibly someone from the Never Trump movement or a Trump detractor like Chris Christie or Nikki Haley .
 View image in fullscreen Vice President JD Vance speaks at a campaign rally on 2 November in Ohio. Photograph: Tom Brenner/Pool Getty Images North America/AP Share 1h ago 12.20 EST What can Democrats do to stop the Iran war?
 Sid in California asked in a reader callout: How can Democrats help stop the Iran war and what are their options to do it? How much time would it take to for Democrats to stop the Iran war and would Trump veto any legislation they pass?
 double quotation mark Chris Stein , senior politics reporter: The first tool Democrats have to force an end to the war with Iran is a war powers resolution. If they don’t try to force one through Congress before this year ends, they may do so next year, when they will officially take control of the House and Senate. But such resolutions don’t have much of a track record of working, at least not under Trump — the president has ignored the one that Democrats passed earlier this year with a handful of Republican votes. And so it’s likely that Democrats will take more forceful action, such as holding up funding for the defense department to force Trump into ending the war. There are a few different avenues to do that, potentially even before the new Congress begins in January. We’ll see how it turns out.
 Will the Iran war cost Trump in the US midterm elections? Your questions answered Read more View image in fullscreen Iranians gather next to a huge anti-Trump billboard at the Enghelab square during an anti-US and Israeli protest gathering in Tehran on 4 November. Photograph: Abedin Taherkenareh/EPA Share 1h ago 12.11 EST What does impeachment look like in the Senate with Democratic majority?
 Grauniad9999 asks in the comments: With the Democrat Senate majority and the likelihood of Maga / Republican splintering, what is the odds of achieving impeachment numbers in the Senate?
 double quotation mark Lauren Gambino , senior political correspondent : I think it would very much depend on who was being impeached. There is a lot of anger at the defense Sec. Hegseth. And we could have an early test of who might be willing to side with Democrats on an impeachment if Congressman Massie, the Kentucky Republican who lost his primary to a Trump-backed rival, does move forward with impeachment articles against Hegseth, as he’s said he’ll do. Massie will leave office in January, so this would be brought in final days of the outgoing Congress. He’d just need 218 votes and then it’d get sent to the Senate. As for impeachment against Trump, that is a trickier question that Democrats are wrestling with, particularly in the House where impeachment articles are brought. Voters made clear on Tuesday they wanted to punish Trump and put a check on his agenda. And of course many Democrats, and a few Republicans, feel he’s committed high crimes and misdemeanors. The opposing view is that impeachment is all-consuming and would distract from their legislative efforts
 View image in fullscreen In an act of civil disobedience, active duty U.S. Air Force Major Jason Watson calls for the impeachment and removal of President Donald Trump on the Capitol steps, in Washington, D.C., U.S., on July 1, 2026. Photograph: Allison Bailey/NurPhoto/Shutterstock Share 1h ago 12.11 EST Will the midterm results affect food and gas prices?
 Dee Kee in California asked in a reader callout: How does it affect me? Will anything affect the cost of food and cost of gas?
 double quotation mark Dominic Rushe , US business editor: Democrats are keen to end the war in Iran and some Republicans - most notably JD Vance - are blaming their losses on the war’s impact on the price of oil. So a resolution to that conflict now looks more likely and traders are already predicting oil prices will come down. That will filter through to prices at the pumps. But it wont be immediate. Food prices are another matter. Inflation is now 3.7% and is rising faster than wages. Trump’s tariffs continue to filter through to consumers. With Trump threatening to veto any bills he does not like, it seems unlikely that Democrats will be able to pass legislation that will meaningfully bring down prices.
 View image in fullscreen Gas prices are displayed at a Love's gas station in Magee, Mississippi, US, November 4, 2026. Photograph: Edgar Su/Reuters Not your imagination: from backpacks to food, consumer goods are getting worse Read more Share 1h ago 12.03 EST Why hasn't Mississippi been called yet?
 In the comments, reader Heavycola asks: Why is the count in Mississippi taking so long?
 double quotation mark Adria R. Walker , a reporter on the race and equity team: As of Thursday, according to Mississippi Secretary of State Michael Watson, there are between 12,000 and 20,000 affidavit ballots that are still uncounted in Mississippi’s Senate race. Because thousands of voters were inaccurately marked inactive, due to the Secretary of State’s office using unverified Experian data, Mississippi received a historic number of affidavit ballots. Voters who cast an affidavit ballot because they didn’t have a photo ID have five days (until 10 November) to cure their ballots. Additionally, there are outstanding mail-in ballots that have until 10 November to reach precincts to be counted. Because the race remains so close, it’s necessary to wait to receive all votes before calling it.
 US midterm elections 2026: live results from Senate, House and governor races in all 50 states Read more View image in fullscreen Scott Colom, the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Mississippi, speaks to reporters about the tight race against Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. Photograph: Lauren Witte/Reuters Share Updated at  12.08 EST 19h ago 18.10 EST Welcome to the conversation
 The 2026 US midterm elections were a forceful rebuke of Donald Trump and the Republicans as Democrats captured control of Congress .
 Democrats hoping for a “blue wave” saw a blue tsunami as they triumphed in deep-red states such as Texas, Kansas and South Carolina to build comfortable majorities in both the Senate and House of Representatives. Voters also elected Democratic governors in Texas, Georgia, Iowa, Wisconsin and Ohio, all states Trump won in 2024.
 Democrats’ blue wave and a bad night for Trump: key US midterms takeaways Read more Over the last month, we’ve been answering your questions in a series of reader conversations from how immigration and the economy’s impact on voters, to who is spending the most on campaigns.
 So how did Democrats pull off the win for Congress, and what’s next for them and for Trump? Join us at noon ET on Friday November 6 , when the Guardian’s political reporters will answer all your questions on the midterms results.
